source.title: Unlearning vs. Obfuscation: Are We Truly Removing Knowledge?
source.authors: Guangzhi Sun; Potsawee Manakul; Xiao Zhan; M. Gales

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are minor PDF text-extraction artifacts, but the relevant text and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly probes whether unlearning methods leave targeted information accessible, using yes/no and multiple-choice questions rather than the original studies’ evaluations. It also tests a fine-tuning attack against DF-MCQ.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for open-ended questions, yes/no probes, MCQ probes, and an SFT attack. I did not treat cited findings from other work as results of this study. Figure 5 reports outcomes for obfuscation sample counts and learning rates, but those values are shown only in plots and are not needed for the main claim verdicts.
record.test_reason: The study uses its own yes/no and MCQ probes to test whether WHP+ (a WHP variant) removes person knowledge or only obfuscates it. It also tests its own counter-method, DF-MCQ, against these probes and an SFT relearning attack. These are different methods aimed at the same question as the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that obfuscation methods (WHP+, NPO) add knowledge rather than remove it, and so fail yes/no and MCQ probes. They conclude that DF-MCQ truly removes the knowledge: over 90% refusal and near-random-choice uncertainty on the probes, with retain sets largely preserved and robustness to an SFT attack.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates WHP+ alongside its own DF-MCQ method. DF-MCQ flattens model output distributions over generated MCQ choices and uses a retain loss; it is not the original gradient-ascent, Harry Potter, or RMU procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by method and probe format. WHP+ retains high accuracy on reference yes/no probes but shows a target-name-related Yes shortcut on in-training and out-of-training splits. DF-MCQ’s reported Qwen2.5 refusal behavior required a higher LoRA rank. The paper also reports that WHP+ shortcut behavior rises with more obfuscation samples and higher learning rates, but those plotted values are not extracted as rows.

fits_no_version.finding: WHP+ learns to answer Yes to any yes/no question naming the target, giving 0.0 accuracy on the wrong-answer splits. The Yes-rate rises with obfuscation samples and learning rate, and correlates 0.84 with unlearning efficacy (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Obfuscation-style unlearning induces a target-name response bias that grows with unlearning strength.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study is limited to person-centric WPU facts and instruction models under 10B parameters, as the authors note. The SFT attack uses questions about other individuals rather than forgotten facts. Yes/no accuracy and entropy vary by split, and WHP+ shows a target-name shortcut that complicates interpreting its split-specific accuracy. The text reports no error bars or confidence intervals for the principal table results.
record.rows_left_out: The NPO open-ended comparison and several Table 2/3 entries are not separately extracted where they do not add evidence about recovery beyond the retained-set and target-set results shown. Table 6’s retain and hard-retain yes/no results, Table 7’s hard-retain results, and Appendix Tables 8–10’s per-subset breakdowns are omitted to keep the record focused on target recovery and within the 60-row limit. Figure 5’s learning-rate and obfuscation-sample results are figure-only and not transcribed. Table 5’s continual-unlearning results do not test recovery from the listed attacks.

untested.parts: WMDP/RMU-style hazardous-knowledge unlearning; general-capability benchmarks. Only person facts (WPU) and ROUGE/MCQ measures are used.
No fine-tuning attack on WHP+ or NPO. The only SFT attack (on DF-MCQ) uses other individuals, not forgotten facts or a subset of them.
No activation-direction ablation or internal analysis; the evidence is behavioural only.
Jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information are not tested. Yes/no and MCQ probes are run only on Llama-3.1-8B.
DF-MCQ is not tested against quantization, activation ablation, relearning on forgotten facts, or jailbreaks. Qwen is evaluated only on open-ended questions.

missing.what: NPO retain ROUGE-L 76.85 and hard-retain 53.85 vs original 91.17/59.62: a general-ability cost.
WHP+ open-ended refusal rates of 9.23% (Llama) and 12.26% (Qwen).

record.verdict_notes:
WHP+ (Liu et al. 2024) is a variant of the original WHP, not the original source, so verdicts on A are allowed. DF-MCQ is the authors' own method, so its rows go to F rather than A or B.

The declared-omitted results show DF-MCQ has its own capability costs:
- hard-retain MCQ accuracy falls 76.73→63.19 (Table 7);
- yes/no hard-retain accuracy falls 45.00→37.34 (Table 6).
The authors admit a 'slight shortcut impact'. These should become rows: they would add a limits_scope on F.

In the Appendix, WHP+ subset 5 scores 71.79 MCQ accuracy vs the original 48.72, showing leakage varies by target. All results are averaged over 5 subsets with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares targeted forgetting and retained-set performance, but does not establish that the reported ROUGE-L values are near-chance targeted-knowledge accuracy. Its attack tests are recorded under B, C, and E.
Tests SFT on questions about other individuals; does not test fine-tuning on forgotten facts or a subset of those facts, nor all unrelated or loosely related training sets.
The paper analyzes obfuscation versus removal using behavioral probes; it does not ablate an activation direction or perform an internal activation edit.
Tests yes/no and MCQ probe formats, including a forced yes/no response. Does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context provision of forgotten information.
DF-MCQ is evaluated against the paper’s probes and an SFT attack. It is not tested against activation ablation or quantization, and the SFT attack is limited to questions about other people.

source_check.notes: All 25 rows match the text. All DF-MCQ results are the authors' own tests with no uncertainty reported; the SFT attack uses other individuals' questions and its size is not given. WHP+ MCQ accuracy varies by subset (18.18-71.79, Table 9): at chance on sets 3-4 and above the original on set 5.
